          What: Recently, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) held its 63rd Monetary Policy

                 1. Global Economy:

                                        i. Global Uncertainty Continues: The global economy is facing uncertainty

                         Despite global challenges, India's economy continues to remain

                      b. Services and Manufacturing Support Growth:

                       Manufacturing activity grew strongly.

                      d. Investment Outlook Remains Positive:

                       High capacity utilisation and strong credit growth are supporting

                     The government's continued focus on infrastructure is also expected

                       e. Challenges Ahead:

                     The West Asia conflict may affect energy prices and supply chains.

                   A weak monsoon and strong El Niño conditions may affect

                       However, adequate foodgrain stocks and government measures are

                               f. Exports Outlook:

                        Services exports are expected to remain strong.

                       Trade agreements are expected to support merchandise exports.

                 3. GDP Growth Outlook: Based on the conditions of the Indian economy, real

              4. Inflation Outlook:

                 CPI inflation increased to 4.8% in August 2026 from 4.5% in July.

                The increase was mainly due to higher food and fuel inflation.

                Core inflation also increased to 4.2%, showing an increase in underlying

                Food price increases have become more widespread, with higher prices of

              5. Inflation Forecast: CPI inflation for 2026–27 is projected at 5.2%.

6. Rationale for Monetary Policy Decisions:

             The RBI explained its policy decision by looking at the outlook for inflation and
             economic growth in India.

                                  i. Inflation needs attention:

                           Inflation is expected to remain higher than last year. The RBI expects
                       headline CPI inflation to average around 5.8% over the next three
                       quarters.

                   Core inflation is also projected at 4.4% for 2026–27, showing that price
                      pressures are not limited to food and fuel alone.

                   The RBI also sees some signs of inflation becoming more widespread.
                       This means the increase in prices could gradually affect more goods and
                        services.

                       Therefore, the RBI felt that inflation needs closer attention, even though
                       the economy continues to grow strongly.

                                 ii. Supply-Side Inflation Risks

                      Higher energy prices and input costs can increase the cost of producing
                   goods and services, putting pressure on inflation.

                           Inflation expectations have also increased to some extent. However,
                       there is limited evidence that businesses are widely passing these higher
                      costs into their prices.

                       This means that supply-side pressures are present, but they have not yet
                  become deeply embedded in the overall pricing process.

                                 iii. Growth Remains Strong:

                      Despite global and geopolitical uncertainties, the Indian economy
                     continues to remain resilient.

                    Growth is broad-based, with different parts of the economy continuing
                         to perform well.

                       At the same time, strong growth in money and credit could create
                    demand-side inflationary pressure. Therefore, the RBI needs to keep a
                       close watch on these developments.

                      iv. Monetary Policy Decision:

                   The decision was taken because inflation risks have increased, even
                     though economic growth remains strong.

                   The MPC changed its stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. This
                  means the RBI is not considering a rate cut in the near term.





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                               6

Depending on how inflation and growth develop, the next move could be
                    a rate hike or a pause.

                    v. RBI Will Watch Inflation Closely

                   The RBI will monitor whether inflation becomes more widespread and
                     whether supply-side pressures start affecting the prices set by
                      businesses.

                              Its main focus remains bringing inflation closer to the target while
                      maintaining economic stability.

                      vi. Members of the MPC meeting:

                          Dr. Nagesh Kumar

                        Shri Saugata Bhattacharya

                          Prof. Ram Singh

                          Dr. Poonam Gupta

                        Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya

                The next meeting of the MPC is scheduled for December 2 to 4, 2026.

            (C) Concept corner:

                                i. Consumer Price Index (CPI) Inflation: It measures the increase in the prices
                   of goods and services commonly purchased by consumers, such as food,
                     clothing, housing, transport, and healthcare.

                Example: If the CPI inflation is 4%, it means the avg. cost of a basket of
                consumer goods and services has increased by 4% compared to the
                  previous year.

                                ii. Core Inflation: It measures inflation excluding food and fuel prices, as these
                   prices are highly volatile (changing frequently and unpredictably). It reflects
                   the underlying trend in inflation.

                  The underlying trend is the real or basic pattern after removing
                    temporary or short-term changes. In inflation, it refers to the actual
                       direction of inflation after excluding items whose prices change a lot (like
                     food and fuel).

                Example: If food prices rise sharply due to poor rainfall but prices of most
                   other goods remain stable, core inflation may remain low even though overall
                      inflation increases.

                               iii. Headline Inflation: It is the overall inflation rate that includes all items in the
               Consumer Price Index (CPI), including food and fuel.

                Example: If higher food and fuel prices push CPI inflation to 4.5%, then
                  headline inflation is 4.5%.





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                               7

iv. Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): The LAF is a tool used by the RBI to
               manage short-term liquidity (money supply) in the banking system. Under the
                  LAF, the RBI:

                   Lends money to banks through the Repo Rate when banks need funds.

                    Borrows money from banks through the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) to
                    absorb excess liquidity.

                Example: If banks are short of funds, they borrow from the RBI at the Repo
                   Rate. If banks have surplus funds, they deposit them with the RBI under the
                 SDF.

                   v. Repo Rate (under LAF): The Repo Rate is the interest rate at which the RBI
                 lends short-term funds to banks against government securities under the
                    Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF).

                Example: If the RBI raises the repo rate, borrowing becomes more expensive
                     for banks, which may increase loan interest rates for customers.

                      vi. Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): It is the rate at which the RBI accepts
                  overnight deposits from banks without providing any collateral. It helps
                 absorb excess liquidity from the banking system.

                Example: If banks have surplus funds, they can park the money with the RBI
                and earn interest at the SDF rate.

                       vii. Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): It is the facility through which scheduled
                 commercial banks can borrow overnight funds from the RBI by pledging
                government securities, usually at a rate higher than the repo rate.

                Example: If a bank faces an unexpected shortage of funds at the end of the
                   day, it can borrow from the RBI through the MSF.

                       viii. Bank Rate: It is the interest rate at which the RBI lends money to banks for
                  the long term without any repurchase agreement. It is also linked to certain
                  penalty charges under RBI regulations.

                Example: An increase in the Bank Rate generally signals tighter monetary
                   conditions and may lead to higher borrowing costs in the economy.

                      ix. Fixed Reverse Repo Rate: It is the interest rate at which the RBI borrows
               money from banks against government securities for a short period. When
                banks have surplus funds, they can lend them to the RBI and earn interest at
                   the reverse repo rate.

                Example: If banks have excess cash and park ₹1,000 crore with the RBI at the
                 Reverse Repo Rate, they earn interest while the excess money is temporarily
                 withdrawn from the banking system.





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                               8

Note: The RRR continues to exist at 3.35%, but it is no longer used for day-
                  to-day liquidity management.

                    After the introduction of the SDF, banks prefer to park their surplus funds
                   with the RBI through the SDF, as it offers a higher interest rate (5.00%) and
                does not require collateral. As a result, the Fixed Reverse Repo Rate has
               become largely redundant, although it has not been discontinued.

                    x. Supply-side measures: These are steps taken by the government to
                  increase the supply of goods and services or reduce supply disruptions,
                   helping control inflation.

                Examples:

                      Releasing food grains from buffer stocks.

                      Importing essential commodities.

                     Promoting crop diversification.

                     Improving storage and transport facilities.

                      xi. Demand-side measures: These are actions taken mainly by the RBI to reduce
                   or increase demand in the economy by changing interest rates and liquidity.

                Examples:

                      Increasing the repo rate to reduce borrowing and control inflation.

                    Reducing the repo rate to encourage borrowing and support economic
                      growth.

                       xii. MPC Stance: It refers to the approach taken by the RBI's MPC in guiding
                     interest rates and liquidity conditions to achieve macroeconomic objectives
                       like price stability, economic growth, and financial stability. The key stances
                     are:

                  Accommodative stance: This indicates that the RBI is willing to lower
                         interest rates or keep them low to support economic growth. This
                    approach is typically adopted during periods of economic slowdown
                 when demand needs a boost. By ensuring easy liquidity and encouraging
                      borrowing, the central bank aims to stimulate investment and
                     consumption.

                A hawkish or tightening stance, on the other hand, is adopted when
                         inflationary pressures are high. In this case, the RBI focuses on controlling
                          inflation by increasing interest rates or reducing excess liquidity in the
                     system. This makes borrowing costlier, which in turn slows down
                     excessive spending and curbs inflation.

                A calibrated tightening stance means the RBI intends to gradually
                    withdraw monetary accommodation and move towards a tighter monetary





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                               9

policy, depending on economic conditions. Here, the RBI wants to reduce
                    excess monetary support without tightening policy more than necessary.

                                           It differs from a hawkish stance in that calibrated tightening focuses
                      on the gradual and measured withdrawal of monetary support,
                      whereas a hawkish stance indicates a stronger preference for
                            controlling inflation, which may involve raising interest rates or
                        keeping them high for longer.

                A dovish or easing stance is similar to an accommodative stance but
                       signals a clearer preference for interest rate cuts. This stance is used
                 when inflation is under control, and economic growth needs stimulation.
                  By reducing borrowing costs and increasing credit flow, the RBI aims to
                     boost consumer spending and investment.

                      Neutral Stance: This stance in monetary policy means the RBI's MPC is
                        neither inclined towards increasing nor decreasing interest rates shortly.
                      This stance indicates that future rate changes will depend on economic
                       data, such as inflation trends, GDP growth, and financial stability. It
                      provides flexibility to adjust policy as needed while maintaining a
                    balanced approach to inflation control and economic growth.

     Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies

          What: This statement comes along with the RBI’s MPC. In the statement, the RBI
          announced 2 important measures to improve customer convenience and strengthen
          engagement with financial market participants. The RBI will:

                Introduce interoperability among NBFC-Account Aggregators (NBFC-AAs),
                allowing customers to access and share their financial information through an
            NBFC-AA of their choice.

                  Facilitate the inclusion of bank deposit information in the Consolidated
             Account Statement (CAS) through NBFC-AAs, helping customers view more of
                  their financial information in one place.

                Constitute a Technical Consultative Committee for Financial Markets to
                   facilitate structured discussions with market participants on policy and
                operational issues relating to financial markets.

         Why: These measures aim to make it easier for customers to access and share their
             financial information and view different financial assets in one place. The





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                              10

committee will help the RBI engage with market participants on policy and
            operational issues relating to financial markets.

              Tell me more:

            (A) Initiatives under the statement are explained below:

                 1. Measures to Enhance Customer Convenience through the Account
                 Aggregator Framework:

               The RBI wants to make the Account Aggregator (AA) system easier to use.
                   At present, customers use AAs to access and share their financial
                    information. The new changes will give customers more flexibility in
                choosing an AA and make it easier to see their financial information in one
                   place.

                                        i. Any NBFC-AA can be used: Customers will be able to access and share
                          their financial information from different Financial Information Providers
                       (FIPs) through any NBFC-AA of their choice. This is possible because of
                         interoperability among NBFC-AAs.

                                       ii. Bank deposits can be shown in CAS: SEBI-regulated depositories will be
                          facilitated to include bank deposit information in the Consolidated
                   Account Statement (CAS) through NBFC-AAs.

                                       iii. One place for investments and deposits: A demat account holder will be
                      able to see both demat holdings and bank deposits in the same CAS.

                           iv. Customers without demat accounts: Even customers who do not have a
                   demat account can continue to get and share a consolidated view of
                        their financial information through NBFC-AAs.

                        v. These measures are expected to be implemented by December 31, 2026.

                 2. Constitution of the Financial Market Consultative Committee (FMCC):

               The RBI has decided to constitute a Technical Consultative Committee for
                   Financial Markets. The committee will provide a platform for the RBI to
                engage with market participants and other stakeholders on policy and
                   operational matters relating to:

                 Money markets

                   Government securities markets

                      Foreign exchange markets

                      Related derivative markets

                        Financial market infrastructure

               The composition and terms of reference of the committee will be notified
                    separately.





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                              11

(B) Concept Corner:

                 1. Account Aggregator (AA): An AA is an entity regulated by the RBI that helps
                 customers access and share their financial information digitally, with the
                  customer's consent.

                 2. NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA): An NBFC-AA is an NBFC that is
                  authorised by the RBI to provide Account Aggregator services.

                 3. Financial Information Provider (FIP): An FIP is an institution that holds a
                 customer's financial information. For example, a bank acts as an FIP for the
                  customer's bank account information.

                 4. Interoperability: It means that different NBFC-AAs can work with the same
                    financial information providers. This allows a customer to choose any
                    participating AA to access and share their financial information.

                 5. Consolidated Account Statement (CAS): CAS gives an investor a single
                 statement showing their investments held in different securities accounts.
                Under the new measure, information about bank deposits can also be
                  included, giving customers a more complete view of their financial assets.

     RBI Amends Directions on Acquisition and Holding of
     Shares

          What: Recently, the RBI issued the RBI Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting
            Rights Amendment Directions, 2026, with immediate effect.

             The amendment allows eligible mutual funds, insurance companies and pension
              funds to obtain one-time approval from the RBI for subsequent acquisitions of
              major shareholding. Earlier, prior approval was required again when an
                 investor's aggregate sharehoing fell below 5% after an initial acquisition of major
                shareholding.

         Why: The RBI reviewed the existing approval requirements and decided to simplify
            the process for eligible institutional investors making subsequent acquisitions. The
          change provides a one-time approval facility while retaining regulatory oversight
           over significant shareholdings in banks.

              Tell me more:

            (A) Background:





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                              12

Banks accept deposits from the public, so the RBI closely monitors who owns
                  their shares and who can influence their decisions. If an investor acquires a
                 significant shareholding in a bank, it may gain greater influence over the bank’s
            management and decision-making. Therefore, RBI approval is required for certain
              major acquisitions of shares or voting rights in banks.

             (B) About the development:

                 1. Applicability:

               The directions are applied to:

                                        i. Commercial Banks.

                                       ii. Small Finance Banks (SFBs).

                                       iii. Payment Banks (PBs).

                           iv. Local Area Banks (LABs).

                 2. Who can get one-time approval?

               The RBI has extended this facility to 3 types of institutional investors. These
                  are financial institutions that manage and invest money collected from
                     individuals.

               The RBI allows eligible institutions from these three categories to apply for
                 one-time approval for subsequent major purchases of shares in a bank.

                    Mutual funds: Collect money from investors and invest it in shares, bonds
                   and other financial assets. They are regulated by SEBI.

                    Insurance companies: Collect premiums from policyholders and invest
                     these funds to meet future insurance claims. They are regulated by IRDAI.

                    Pension funds: Manage and invest money to provide retirement benefits
                        to subscribers. They are regulated by PFRDA.

                 3. New rule:

                To understand the amendment, remember that buying a significant stake in a
                bank is different from buying shares in an ordinary company. A large
                  shareholding can give an investor greater influence over the bank. Therefore,
                   the RBI regulates such acquisitions.

               The amendment makes it easier for eligible institutional investors to make
                 subsequent major share purchases without having to repeat the approval
                 process each time, provided they obtain the required one-time approval and
                    follow the RBI’s conditions.

                                       The investor must obtain prior RBI approval before

                                                    RBI’s conditions.

                                                        rights.

                       Cancellation of approval   violated or the investor or an associated person is

                 4. 5% reporting rule:

               The RBI wants to keep track of changes in the shareholding of investors
                 covered by the amendment. For this purpose, it has introduced a reporting
                  requirement linked to the 5% shareholding level.

                             If a covered investor’s total shareholding in a bank falls below 5% or rises
                above 5%, the investor must inform both the RBI and the concerned bank
                    within three working days of the change.

                Example: Suppose an eligible mutual fund holds 6% of the shares in ABC
                  Bank.

                                   If its shareholding falls from 6% to 4.8%, it must report the change.

                                   If its shareholding rises from 4.8% to 5.2%, it must also report the
                    change.

                      In both cases, the information must be provided to the RBI and ABC Bank
                    within three working days.

               Remember: The reporting threshold is 5%, and the reporting deadline is 3
                working days. This requirement applies to investors covered by the
                amendment, not automatically to every shareholder of every bank.

                 5. Amendment about portfolio managers:

                  RBI rules regulate the acquisition of significant shareholdings in banks. This
                    raises an important question: When a portfolio manager helps a client buy
                bank shares, should that purchase also be counted as an acquisition by the
                     portfolio manager?





RBI 247 October 2026                                                                                                              14

The amendment clarifies that the client's purchase will not be treated as an
                     indirect acquisition by the portfolio manager if three conditions are met:

                                        i. The client owns the shares: The shares belong to the client, and the
                          client has the right to exercise the voting rights attached to them.

                                       ii. The manager only gives advice: The portfolio manager can recommend
                     buying or selling shares, but the client is not required to follow that
                       advice.

                                       iii. Voting follows the client's instructions: If the portfolio manager votes on
                      the client's behalf, it must do so according to the client's specific
                         instructions.

                Example: Suppose a client asks a portfolio manager for advice on buying
                  shares in ABC Bank. The client owns the shares, decides whether to follow
                   the manager's advice, and retains control over voting rights. If all three
                   conditions are met, the client's purchase is not treated as an indirect
                 purchase by the portfolio manager under this provision.

                 6. How can investors apply?

                      Eligible investors must submit their application through PRAVAAH, the RBI’s
                    online portal for regulatory applications. The RBI then reviews the application
                and may approve or reject it.

     RBI Issues Master Direction on Note Sorting Machines

          What: Recently, the RBI issued the Master Direction on Note Sorting Machines
           (NSM), consolidating and updating its existing instructions on the authentication and
             fitness sorting of banknotes. The Direction was issued under Sections 35A and 56
            of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

           A key requirement is that banks must phase out NSM models that have been
               discontinued from production by June 30, 2027. Going forward, banks must
               procure only NSMs certified by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).

         Why: Banks handle large volumes of cash every day. Before banknotes are reissued
             to customers, banks need to ensure that the notes are genuine and in sufficiently
          good physical condition for recirculation.

          Manual checking of every note is time-consuming. Note Sorting Machines help
          banks identify suspected counterfeit notes and separate damaged or worn-out
           notes from those suitable for recirculation.

              Tell me more:

            (A) Key Provisions of the Master Direction:
